facts.raw_span: A 60-year-old Saudi man presented with an 18-month history of erythroderma affecting his entire body and face
slightly pruritic, slowly progressive erythematous lesions on his trunk and retroauricular area
confluent lichenified erythromelanotic plaques with overlying thick greasy scales on the face, neck, trunk, genitalia, upper and lower extremities, palms, and soles
sparing of the nails and scalp
Bilateral lower‐lid ectropion was present
no palpable lymphadenopathy
epidermotropism of a large number of atypical lymphocytes—single and in clusters—and a superficial dermal band‐like lymphocytic infiltrate with dermal fibrosis
Direct immunofluorescence was negative for fibrinogen, C3, IgA, IgM, and IgG
Immunohistochemical staining showed tumor cells positive for CD3 and CD45RO but negative for CD4, CD8, and CD7
CD30 was positive in fewer than 25% of lymphocytes

slightly pruritic, slowly progressive erythematous lesions on his trunk and retroauricular area
confluent lichenified erythromelanotic plaques with overlying thick greasy scales on the face, neck, trunk, genitalia, upper and lower extremities, palms, and soles
sparing of the nails and scalp
Bilateral lower‐lid ectropion was present
no palpable lymphadenopathy
epidermotropism of a large number of atypical lymphocytes—single and in clusters—and a superficial dermal band‐like lymphocytic infiltrate with dermal fibrosis
Direct immunofluorescence was negative for fibrinogen, C3, IgA, IgM, and IgG
Immunohistochemical staining showed tumor cells positive for CD3 and CD45RO but negative for CD4, CD8, and CD7
CD30 was positive in fewer than 25% of lymphocytes

concepts.why: The patient's presentation of erythroderma, lichenified erythromelanotic plaques, and atypical lymphocytes on skin biopsy is consistent with Sézary syndrome, a subtype of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.
The patient's history of slowly progressive erythematous lesions and the presence of atypical lymphocytes on skin biopsy support a diagnosis of mycosis fungoides, a type of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.
The patient's presentation of erythroderma and atypical lymphocytes on skin biopsy is consistent with cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, but the specific subtype is not clear.
The patient's presentation of erythroderma is a non-specific finding that could be due to various causes, including inflammatory skin disorders.
The patient's skin biopsy findings of atypical lymphocytes and the presence of CD30-positive cells support a diagnosis of lymphomatoid papulosis, a type of cutaneous lymphoma.
It explains the presence of bilateral lower-lid ectropion and negative direct immunofluorescence results in the context of erythroderma and atypical lymphocytes.

rationales.F01: Erythroderma is a common presentation of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma
rationales.F03: Confluent lichenified erythromelanotic plaques are characteristic of mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome
rationales.F05: Bilateral lower-lid ectropion can be seen in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma
rationales.F07: Epidermotropism of atypical lymphocytes is a hallmark of mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome
rationales.F09: Immunohistochemical staining positive for CD3 and CD45RO is consistent with cutaneous T-cell lymphoma
rationales.F10: CD30 positivity in fewer than 25% of lymphocytes is more characteristic of lymphomatoid papulosis
